resources.title: DCP 4300 / URP 6931: Artificial Intelligence in the Built Environment
resources.description: The Fall 2024 syllabus combines computational foundations, urban data structures, and AI applications for the built environment. It introduces Python and cloud notebooks before examining numeric, image, network, and text data. Neural-network and language-model topics connect to urban mobility, property values, energy, sustainability, and community development. Labs and a final project provide an example of how a planning program can organize practical AI teaching around multiple kinds of urban evidence.
resources.method: Artificial neural networks; Convolutional neural networks; Graph neural networks; Large language models
resources.contributor: Shenhao Wang (Fall 2024 syllabus)
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Planning, design, engineering, and data science students and instructors

resources.title: Urban Data Science
resources.description: This online teaching resource combines lectures, readings, exercises, and projects for urban data analysis. Its modules cover APIs, web scraping, data preparation, spatial relationships, classification, clustering, and text analysis. Planning examples draw on transit, housing, and equity. The course also asks learners to consider bias, causal inference, and the limitations of data science. Public materials support independent learning, while some syllabus and collaboration services are reserved for enrolled UCLA students.
resources.method: Machine learning; Classification; Clustering; Natural language processing
resources.contributor: Adam Millard-Ball
resources.license: CC BY-NC 4.0, as identified by the course site's linked Creative Commons license; check separately credited material
resources.audience: Planning students, instructors, and independent urban data science learners

resources.title: URP 4702: AI Applications in Design & Planning
resources.description: The syllabus describes an undergraduate introduction to AI and geodesign, linking GIS and stakeholder-informed planning with simulation and predictive technologies. Students examine machine learning, generative AI, and digital twins through readings, discussions, case studies, and a group project. Its learning objectives include evaluating ethical and social issues alongside technical capabilities. The document provides an example of a concept-focused planning course that connects emerging tools to urban challenges rather than assuming a specialized computer science background.
resources.method: Machine learning; Generative AI; Digital twins
resources.contributor: Stephanie Wakefield; Jun Wang
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Undergraduate planning and design students; instructors developing AI curricula

resources.title: PPDE 642: Advanced Urban Analytics
resources.description: Advanced Urban Analytics is the second course in a USC urban data science sequence. Its public repository contains instructional materials, assignments, software guidance, and syllabi using Python and Jupyter notebooks. The documented scope includes spatial and network analysis, spatial models, and applied machine learning. The course assumes PPD 534 or equivalent preparation. It offers planning instructors examples of reproducible computational teaching and provides learners with materials they can inspect and adapt under the repository's stated license.
resources.method: Applied machine learning; Python; Jupyter notebooks
resources.contributor: Geoff Boeing
resources.license: MIT License for repository content, subject to any separately identified third-party material
resources.audience: Graduate planning students and instructors with introductory urban data science preparation

resources.title: Urban AI: AI-Driven Decision Support for Real-World Urban Challenges
resources.description: Michigan State University’s official AI-Ready Spartans announcement identifies Urban AI as a 2026 award in its Non-credit Learning Experiences category. The project connects artificial intelligence with planning and urban development and names Si Chen as its faculty lead. It provides an example of a university-supported initiative intended to build responsible AI decision-support skills. The institutional announcement identifies a 2026–2027 launch cycle; detailed delivery arrangements should be checked with the university.
resources.method: AI-driven decision support; responsible AI
resources.contributor: Si Chen
resources.license: Not stated; link to the official university announcement
resources.audience: Students and instructors interested in AI-supported planning and urban development

resources.title: MUSA 5080 / CPLN 5920: Public Policy Analytics
resources.description: Public Policy Analytics introduces data science and machine learning for planning and policy applications through lectures, demonstrations, labs, assignments, and projects. Its public-sector perspective connects analytical performance to governance, public goods, equity, and algorithmic bias. Applications span transportation, housing, public health, land use, and criminal justice. The official course overview identifies R as the teaching language and prior GIS experience as preparation, providing a useful model for integrating computational analysis with substantive planning concerns.
resources.method: Machine learning; Spatial analysis; R
resources.contributor: Elizabeth Delmelle
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Graduate planning and urban spatial analytics students with GIS experience

resources.title: PLAN 6113: Exploring Urban Data with Machine Learning
resources.description: This three-point urban planning course addresses the challenges created by large and complex urban datasets. It combines practical work in preparing data, applying machine learning, and visualizing results with critical discussion of technology in planning. Students are expected to describe, model, and evaluate their analyses alongside historical and theoretical perspectives on technocracy. The official Spring 2026 listing identifies Jonathan Stiles as instructor and classifies the course as an urban planning analytics elective.
resources.method: Machine learning; Data preparation; Data visualization
resources.contributor: Jonathan Stiles
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Graduate urban planning students and instructors teaching computational planning methods

resources.title: 1.C01 / 1.C51: Machine Learning for Sustainable Systems
resources.description: Machine Learning for Sustainable Systems builds on a common machine-learning core and applies analytical methods to cities, urban services, and environmental systems. Case domains include transportation, energy, water, environmental monitoring, infrastructure sensing, climate adaptation, and disaster resilience. Projects focus on identifying insights or decisions that can support sustainability. Undergraduate and graduate versions are cross-listed with urban planning. The catalog describes a spring, second-half-term schedule and additional work for students in the graduate version.
resources.method: Machine learning; Urban data modeling
resources.contributor: Saurabh Amin
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Undergraduate and graduate students with the required machine-learning core and quantitative preparation

resources.title: INFO 5430: AI for Urban Data
resources.description: AI for Urban Data provides a framework for working with urban datasets and choosing analytical techniques for policy problems. The official roster describes data mining, machine learning, GIS, network analysis, simulation, agent-based modeling, and visualization, together with optimization and simulation models. Learning outcomes include finding relevant open data, processing different data formats, and critically evaluating quality, privacy, and bias. The Fall 2026 listing identifies a three-credit, in-person Cornell Tech section with INFO 5410 as prerequisite.
resources.method: Machine learning; Data mining; Agent-based modeling; Simulation
resources.contributor: W. Leon (as listed in the roster)
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Cornell Tech graduate students with INFO 5410 preparation; instructors reviewing urban AI curricula

resources.title: CUSP-GX 8873: Urban Computing and Artificial Intelligence
resources.description: The three-credit course introduces AI techniques for urban data science and asks students to evaluate their societal implications. Its catalog description begins with deep learning for spatial and temporal data, then moves to generative AI, GPT, and large language models for urban governance and modeling. The concluding topics include fairness, bias, causal inference, and urban complexity. The bulletin identifies spring as the typical term but does not name an instructor or confirm a particular section.
resources.method: Deep learning; Generative AI; Large language models; Causal inference
resources.contributor: Not stated in catalog entry
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Graduate urban science students and planning instructors reviewing advanced urban AI teaching

resources.title: CSE 8803 IUC: Introduction to Urban Computing
resources.description: Introduction to Urban Computing studies computational methods for storing, processing, and extracting information from city data. The Spring 2023 course combines machine-learning foundations with network analysis, spatial models, trajectory mining, time series, and visual analytics. Applications cover urban transportation, epidemiology, public health, environmental monitoring, sustainability, and economics. The university-hosted instructor site provides an outline, policies, assignments, and resource links. B. Aditya Prakash is identified as instructor; the archive does not establish a current offering.
resources.method: Machine learning; Network science; Trajectory mining; Time-series analysis
resources.contributor: B. Aditya Prakash
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Graduate computing and urban data students; instructors reviewing computational urban curricula

resources.title: CY PLAN C88: Data Science for Smart Cities
resources.description: This undergraduate connector course introduces data generated by city infrastructures, residents, and sensing systems. Its catalog objectives include machine-learning classification, regression, urban decision-making, and scenario generation. Students examine how analytical methods can support transport, energy, communications, and other urban services while questioning the actionability of results. The archived official catalog lists a two-unit course, cross-listing with civil engineering, and preparation through the foundational data science course. Current scheduling requires separate confirmation.
resources.method: Machine-learning classification; Regression modeling; Urban sensor analytics
resources.contributor: Gonzalez (as identified in catalog)
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Undergraduate students with foundations of data science; planning and engineering instructors

resources.title: UT 439: Urban AI
resources.description: Urban AI prepares students to use emerging AI tools while evaluating their consequences for planning and urban technology. Weekly lectures and programming labs introduce machine-learning basics, language processing, large language models, and human-in-the-loop approaches. Students examine technical, regulatory, environmental, equity, and safety issues before developing their own projects. The Winter 2026 official listing names Xiaofan Liang, describes a three-credit elective, and requires programming knowledge, with Python as the main language. Prior AI experience is not required.
resources.method: Generative AI; Machine learning; Natural language processing; Human-in-the-loop AI
resources.contributor: Xiaofan Liang
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Urban technology and planning students with programming preparation

resources.title: AI, Machine Learning, and the Built Environment: Fundamentals & Proptech Applications
resources.description: This nontechnical executive-education program helps built-environment professionals evaluate and plan AI applications. The three-day learning format combines preparatory readings, lectures, group discussions, and conceptual exercises. Content includes data acquisition, neural-network training, language models, ethics, and implementation. Past examples involve property valuation, floorplans, recommendations, and listing automation. Participants develop an application with peers and learn to manage a technical project. The page identifies Jose Luis Garcia del Castillo y Lopez; registration is currently marked closed.
resources.method: Machine learning; Large language models; AI workflow design
resources.contributor: Jose Luis Garcia del Castillo y Lopez
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Planners, architects, landscape designers, real estate and proptech professionals

resources.title: GGIS 527: Geospatial Artificial Intelligence & Machine Learning
resources.description: GGIS 527 examines the intersection of AI and geospatial analysis through practical interaction with spatial datasets. Students learn machine-learning tools, including decision trees and support vector machines, for finding patterns, categories, clusters, and anomalies. The official description connects these methods to urban planning, sustainable development, geography, economics, agriculture, and other fields. The Fall 2026 roster identifies a four-credit graduate course requiring GGIS 407 or equivalent. An instructor is not identified in the retrieved roster text.
resources.method: Geospatial AI; Decision trees; Support vector machines
resources.contributor: Not stated in retrieved roster
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Graduate geography, GIS, and planning students with GGIS 407 or equivalent preparation

resources.title: PA 470: AI & Machine Learning
resources.description: PA 470 introduces public-sector applications of artificial intelligence and machine learning. The catalog describes a progression from philosophical foundations to major learning frameworks. It is offered through public administration within UIC’s College of Urban Planning and Public Affairs and is relevant to civic analytics, government, and public-policy education. The listing assigns three undergraduate or four graduate credits and specifies prior quantitative preparation plus program admission or instructor consent. An instructor and term are not stated.
resources.method: Artificial intelligence; Machine learning; Public-sector analytics
resources.contributor: Not stated in catalog entry
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Civic analytics, public administration, and public-policy students with required preparation

resources.title: GEOG 495/428: Geospatial Artificial Intelligence
resources.description: These public course materials combine geospatial machine learning, deep learning, and language models with critical analysis of inequality. Labs address housing prices, Seattle urban heat, tree-canopy segmentation, and language-based mapping. Readings and a final essay ask students to examine bias, hallucinations, and the environmental costs of AI. The official university laboratory links to this instructor-maintained syllabus. A Summer 2025 offering is documented; the separately advertised Summer 2026 section was later withdrawn.
resources.method: Geospatial machine learning; Deep learning; Large language models; Computer vision
resources.contributor: Bo Zhao
resources.license: Repository identifies LGPL-2.1; separately credited readings and third-party materials may have other terms.

resources.title: CRP 386: AI in Planning
resources.description: This graduate planning workshop introduces AI and machine learning through practical urban problems and a collaborative project. Students examine applications in land use, transportation, sustainability, and public engagement, alongside social inequity and ethical questions. The syllabus identifies KNIME for data analysis and predictive algorithms, geospatial software for spatial data, and Power BI for communicating findings. GIS knowledge is required. The archived Spring 2025 document names Julio Carrillo as instructor and provides the project sequence.

resources.title: GEOG 398: Aerial Imagery Analysis and Geospatial Machine Learning
resources.description: This four-credit geography course combines interpretation of aerial images with image-based geospatial machine learning. The official catalog identifies applications involving land use, vegetation, structures, urban and industrial patterns, and archaeological sites. Lecture and laboratory sessions develop skills for recognizing and evaluating natural and cultural features. These methods offer planning learners an example of using imagery to build spatial evidence about development and landscapes. Remote sensing and GIS preparation are required; an instructor and term are not listed.
resources.method: Image-based geospatial machine learning; Aerial imagery interpretation
resources.contributor: Not stated in catalog entry
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Upper-level geography, GIS, and planning students with remote-sensing and GIS preparation

resources.title: GEOG 621: Introduction to GeoAI
resources.description: Introduction to GeoAI connects geospatial science with AI through satellite images, spatial point data, and spatiotemporal information. The course emphasizes conceptual understanding and workflows requiring little or no coding. Documented applications include urban analytics, public health, environmental monitoring, and disaster response. Maryland’s official Spring 2027 schedule lists a three-credit online section taught by Ruohan Li. Prior GIS or spatial-analysis coursework is expected, and participation outside the Geospatial AI and Healthcare program requires permission.
resources.method: Geospatial AI; Machine learning; Low-code and no-code workflows
resources.contributor: Ruohan Li
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Geospatial AI and Healthcare graduate students; other GIS-prepared learners with program permission

resources.title: Symbiotic Planning Theory: The CORE Framework for Human–AI Cocreation in Urban Planning
resources.description: This article develops symbiotic planning theory through theoretical synthesis and illustrates its CORE framework through Gainesville's shared micromobility program. Community engagement informed binding equity constraints for a deep reinforcement learning model. The contribution concerns governance as well as optimization: it specifies how AI-generated alternatives, public contestation, transparent evaluation, and reauthorization can support accountable planning. The authors identify the limits of a single-city validation and describe extension to other planning fields as requiring further testing.
resources.method: Human–AI collaboration; Deep reinforcement learning
resources.contributor: Zhong-Ren Peng; Kai-Fa Lu; Yanghe Liu; Qing Hou; Qing Zhang
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source
resources.audience: Planning researchers, educators, public-agency planners, and human–AI governance researchers

resources.title: How the marketing of real estate properties explains mortgage applicants by race and income
resources.description: The paper combines longitudinal property advertisements with mortgage-lending information to examine how neighborhood marketing relates to later applicant composition. A semi-supervised algorithm classifies listing text into categories along an investment and disinvestment continuum. The results identify racial differences that persist after accounting for income. It offers planning researchers a concrete example of text classification applied to housing inequality. The underlying historical listing data are proprietary; the authors link classification code, fabricated example data, and other supporting materials separately.
resources.method: Semi-supervised learning; Property-advertisement text classification
resources.contributor: Isabelle Nilsson; Elizabeth C. Delmelle
resources.license: Not stated; link to original source. Linked code and datasets have separate terms.
resources.audience: Housing and neighborhood researchers, planning educators, fair-housing analysts, and urban-data scientists

resources.title: AI-based urban layout generation model
resources.description: UT Austin and Purdue authors develop a generative model for three-dimensional urban layouts using building and city-block geometry. A graph-based variational autoencoder learns a compact representation from North American cities and generates layouts from sparse inputs. The paper tests reconstruction, missing-building inference, weather-model inputs, and indicator-oriented editing. For planners, it presents a research example of rapidly generating and comparing urban-form scenarios, with model outputs requiring contextual review rather than serving as adopted development plans.
resources.method: Graph-based variational autoencoder; generative urban modeling
resources.institution: The University of Texas at Austin
resources.contributor: Liu He, Harsh G. Kamath, Songlin Fei, Dev Niyogi, Daniel Aliaga
resources.license: See source publication and image license separately
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: Aligning LLM with Humans for Travel Choices: A Persona-Based Embedding Learning Approach
resources.description: Michigan researchers investigate how language-model simulations can better reflect observed travel choices. Their framework learns traveler personas from empirical data and uses behavioral embeddings to select prompts for individuals with different characteristics. Tests use the Swissmetro mode-choice dataset and compare individual predictions and aggregate shares with alternative models. The work gives transportation planners a research example of calibrating AI-based behavioral simulations, while making clear that alignment depends on available data and validation in the intended decision context.
resources.method: Large language models; persona inference; embedding learning; mode-choice modeling
resources.contributor: Tianming Liu, Manzi Li, Yafeng Yin
resources.license: See source publication and image license separately
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: A sub-meter resolution urban surface albedo dataset for 34 U.S. cities based on deep learning
resources.description: This study produces detailed maps of urban surface reflectivity for 34 major U.S. cities using deep learning and multiple remote-sensing datasets. U-Net separates impervious and pervious surfaces, while prediction models estimate their albedo. The maps provide environmental evidence for neighborhood-scale heat analysis and urban climate modeling. For planners, the work illustrates how machine learning can turn aerial imagery, building footprints, and other spatial data into inputs for evaluating cooling strategies, while keeping reflectivity distinct from a complete measure of pedestrian thermal comfort.
resources.method: U-Net segmentation; Deep learning regression
resources.contributor: Shengao Yi; Xiaojiang Li; Yixuan Liu; Xinyu Dong; Wei Tu
resources.license: CC BY-NC-ND 4.0 — https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-nc-nd/4.0/
resources.audience: Urban-design researchers, planning educators, urban-perception researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Urban motifs associated with population health
resources.description: The authors combine health indicators, demographic information, geospatial amenities, and street-view evidence across 28,323 U.S. census tracts. A graph deep-learning model examines how urban features and spatial patterns relate to general, physical, and mental health. The analysis identifies differences in the importance of amenities, greenery, and neighborhood form across health dimensions and socioeconomic settings. Planning readers can use the study to understand an interpretable modeling approach for healthy-city questions, while recognizing that the reported relationships are associations rather than proof that individual design interventions cause health gains.
resources.method: Graph deep learning; GNNExplainer
resources.contributor: Winston Yap; Fábio Duarte; Yu Zheng; Kee Moon Jang; Peng Luo; Paolo Vineis; Carlo Ratti; Filip Biljecki
resources.license: Copyright Springer Nature or its licensor; no open figure-reuse license stated.
resources.audience: Urban-design researchers, planning educators, urban-perception researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Transferable human mobility network reconstruction with neuroGravity
resources.description: neuroGravity combines a gravity-model perspective with graph deep learning to reconstruct mobility flows from incomplete observations. The paper evaluates reconstruction within cities and transfer to places with fewer available travel data. It also studies relationships between learned representations, socioeconomic conditions, and urban livability, showing that spatial income segregation affects transferability. Berkeley coauthor Marta González contributes planning and mobility expertise. The research offers a way to study transport demand in data-scarce settings while emphasizing that cross-city model performance depends on local social and spatial conditions.
resources.method: Physics-informed graph neural network
resources.contributor: Jinming Yang; Shaoyu Huang; Zongyuan Huang; Yaohui Jin; Xiaokang Yang; Marta C. González; Yanyan Xu
resources.license: Copyright Springer Nature or its licensor; no open figure-reuse license stated.
resources.audience: Urban-design researchers, planning educators, urban-perception researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Urban planning in the era of large language models
resources.description: This perspective organizes potential uses of large language models around three planning activities: forming concepts, generating plans, and evaluating outcomes. It considers how language-based reasoning and generative capabilities could assist human planners when they combine urban knowledge, design intentions, and evidence. MIT Senseable City Lab researchers contribute alongside collaborators at other institutions. The framework gives instructors and researchers a structured basis for discussing future workflows, without treating model-generated plans as automatically accurate, participatory, or ready for adoption.
resources.method: Large language models; Generative design; Plan evaluation
resources.contributor: Yu Zheng; Fengli Xu; Yuming Lin; Paolo Santi; Carlo Ratti; Qi R. Wang; Yong Li
resources.license: Copyright Springer Nature or its licensor; no open figure-reuse license stated.
resources.audience: Urban-design researchers, planning educators, urban-perception researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Ubiquitous data-driven framework for traffic emission estimation and policy evaluation
resources.description: This paper combines traffic-camera observations, mobile-phone mobility data, fleet information, and emissions factors to estimate vehicular emissions across Manhattan. Computer vision identifies vehicle categories, while the combined framework produces estimates at finer spatial and temporal scales than conventional aggregate inventories. The authors examine the importance of traffic signals, speed variation, and fleet composition and evaluate policy scenarios, including early congestion-pricing effects. The study shows how existing urban sensors can support climate-policy assessment, with results dependent on local data quality, model assumptions, and traffic conditions.
resources.method: Computer vision; Multi-source urban data fusion
resources.contributor: Songhua Hu; Paolo Santi; Tom Benson; Xuesong Zhou; An Wang; Ashutosh Kumar; Carlo Ratti
resources.license: Copyright Springer Nature or its licensor; no open figure-reuse license stated.
resources.audience: Urban-design researchers, planning educators, urban-perception researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Lessons from a Human-in-the-Loop Machine Learning Approach for Identifying Vacant, Abandoned, and Deteriorated Properties in Savannah, Georgia
resources.description: Georgia Tech coauthor Clio Andris collaborated with Michigan and City of Savannah researchers on VADecide, a model for identifying vacant, abandoned, and deteriorated properties. Local experts helped define the task, label examples, examine features, and interpret model behavior. The study compares this process with machine learning without human input and reflects on differences between expert and algorithmic results. It provides a planning-specific account of how civic knowledge, data quality, and collaborative review shape an AI-supported property inventory.
resources.method: Human-in-the-loop machine learning; active learning; interpretable modeling
resources.contributor: Xiaofan Liang, Brian Brainerd, Tara Hicks, Clio Andris
resources.license: See source publication and image license separately
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: Reducing the social inequity of neighborhood visual environment in Los Angeles through computer vision and multi-model machine learning
resources.description: USC-affiliated researchers combine crowdsourced street imagery, computer vision, and several machine-learning models to study differences in the visual environment across Los Angeles neighborhoods. The analysis relates modeled perceptions of safety, beauty, wealth, livability, boredom, and depression to built-environment features and demographic patterns. It identifies potential planning-relevant associations, including the role of canopy density. The paper provides a neighborhood-equity example while requiring care about image coverage, perceived versus measured conditions, and the limits of observational associations.
resources.method: Computer vision; semantic segmentation; random forests; XGBoost; multi-model machine learning
resources.contributor: Siqin Wang, Jooyoung Yoo, Wenhui Cai, Fan Yang, Xiao Huang, Qian Chayn Sun, Shaokun Lyu
resources.license: Publication and figure reuse terms are recorded separately.

resources.title: Built environment interventions for emission mitigation: A machine learning analysis of travel-related CO2 in a developing city
resources.description: Minnesota coauthor Xinyu Cao and collaborators use gradient-boosting decision trees to examine travel-related carbon emissions in Zhongshan, China. Household travel data support comparisons of built-environment predictors and their nonlinear relationships with emissions. The study highlights accessibility to urban centers, population density, and threshold patterns that may matter for land-use and transportation policy. It offers a planning-specific example of interpretable machine learning while avoiding a simple assumption that predictive relationships establish the causal effect of redevelopment.
resources.method: Gradient boosting decision trees; nonlinear response analysis
resources.contributor: Qifan Shao, Wenjia Zhang, Xinyu (Jason) Cao, Jiawen Yang
resources.license: Publication and figure reuse terms are recorded separately.

resources.title: Mapping trees along urban street networks with deep learning and street-level imagery
resources.description: UBC researchers and collaborators develop a method for detecting individual urban trees and estimating their locations from street-level imagery. Mask R-CNN supplies tree-instance masks, while depth estimation and triangulation support geolocation without relying on a separate aerial dataset. Tests across different cities and image sources examine transferability and positional accuracy. For urban forestry and planning, the paper demonstrates a potentially lower-cost inventory approach and the need to validate detection and location errors against field measurements.
resources.method: Mask R-CNN; instance segmentation; monocular depth estimation; triangulation
resources.contributor: Stefanie Lumnitz, Tahia Devisscher, Jerome R. Mayaud, Valentina Radic, Nicholas C. Coops, Verena C. Griess
resources.license: Publication and figure reuse terms are recorded separately.

resources.title: Deep Learning–Based Assessment of Built Environment From Satellite Images and Cardiometabolic Disease Prevalence
resources.description: This cross-sectional study extracts built-environment features from satellite images using convolutional neural networks and relates them to neighborhood cardiometabolic disease prevalence. The authors compare image-based models with demographic and social-determinants information across seven U.S. cities. Catherine Kreatsoulas supplies the verified Harvard affiliation within a broader clinical and public-health collaboration. The paper offers a method for investigating neighborhood conditions at scale, while documenting that within-city predictions can be weaker than citywide comparisons and that observational associations do not establish causal effects.
resources.method: Convolutional neural networks; LightGBM; Random forest
resources.contributor: Zhuo Chen; Jean-Eudes Dazard; Yassin Khalifa; Issam Motairek; Catherine Kreatsoulas; Sanjay Rajagopalan; Sadeer Al-Kindi
resources.license: Copyright 2024 American Medical Association; no open figure-reuse license verified.

resources.title: Urban form and structure explain variability in spatial inequality of property flood risk among US counties
resources.description: Texas A&M researchers examine how urban form and structure relate to unequal property flood risk across 2,567 U.S. counties. They combine urban features, mobility evidence, and property-risk information, using principal components and a classification-and-regression tree to identify combinations associated with different inequality levels. The study links machine-learning interpretation with questions about density, economic activity, centrality, and segregation. Its planning relevance lies in diagnosing spatial patterns and possible intervention pathways, while the observational design requires caution about causal claims and transfer to individual properties.
resources.method: Classification and regression trees; Principal component analysis
resources.contributor: Junwei Ma; Ali Mostafavi
resources.license: CC BY 4.0 — https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: Transfer learning reveals large discrepancies between air and land surface temperatures in cities
resources.description: This Illinois-led paper develops a physics-informed transfer-learning framework for estimating near-surface urban air temperature where representative measurements are scarce. Its Urban High-Resolution Air Temperature dataset covers 384 cities in the contiguous United States and enables comparisons with satellite land-surface temperatures. The study demonstrates why the two temperature measures can yield different estimates of heat intensity and spatial variability. Planning users can draw on the work for heat-exposure assessment, energy analysis, and climate adaptation while retaining the distinction between modeled air temperature, surface temperature, and personal thermal experience.
resources.method: Physics-informed transfer learning
resources.contributor: Yiwen Zhang; Lei Zhao; TC Chakraborty; Priyam Mazumdar; Keer Zhang; Pierre Gentine
resources.license: CC BY 4.0 — https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: Multimodal deep learning from satellite and street-level imagery for measuring income, overcrowding, and environmental deprivation in urban areas
resources.description: This paper combines satellite and street-level imagery in deep-learning models to estimate fine-scale income, overcrowding, and environmental deprivation. Its London experiments compare image modalities and evaluate predicted spatial patterns against observed indicators. Michael Brauer has a published University of Washington affiliation within the international research team. For urban planning, the study illustrates how complementary visual data can help characterize inequalities when conventional spatial evidence is limited, while emphasizing that image timing, coverage, transferability, and ground-truth quality constrain the interpretation of modeled neighborhood indicators.
resources.method: Multimodal deep learning; Convolutional neural networks
resources.contributor: Esra Suel; Samir Bhatt; Michael Brauer; Seth Flaxman; Majid Ezzati
resources.license: CC BY 4.0 — https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/
resources.audience: Planning researchers, students, and practitioners

resources.title: CitySurfaces: City-scale semantic segmentation of sidewalk materials
resources.description: This journal article introduces CitySurfaces, a computer-vision framework for locating and classifying sidewalk paving materials in street-level images. Active learning guides additional annotation and model refinement, while semantic segmentation distinguishes eight material classes. Training uses Boston and New York imagery, and tests examine transfer to other cities. The research connects pavement inventories with heat, drainage, and pedestrian-environment questions. It also identifies limitations from shadows, occlusion, and incomplete sidewalk-network geometry, so the maps require local validation before informing planning decisions.
resources.method: Active learning; Semantic segmentation; Hierarchical multi-scale attention; Computer vision
resources.contributor: Maryam Hosseini; Fabio Miranda; Jianzhe Lin; Claudio T. Silva
resources.license: © 2022 Elsevier Ltd. All rights reserved. No open article reuse license stated in the published PDF.
resources.audience: Planning researchers, urban infrastructure analysts, urban climate researchers, and computer-vision scholars

resources.title: Mapping the walk: A scalable computer vision approach for generating sidewalk network datasets from aerial imagery
resources.description: This paper introduces TILE2NET, an open-source computer-vision workflow that extracts sidewalks, crosswalks, and footpaths from aerial imagery and converts the results into pedestrian networks. The authors train and evaluate the approach using cities in the northeastern United States, comparing detected infrastructure with available reference data. Claudio Silva supplies the verified NYU affiliation within a wider urban-planning and visualization collaboration. The study addresses gaps in pedestrian data needed for walkability analysis and routing, while reporting limitations related to imagery, obstruction, and network completeness.

resources.title: Predicting human mobility flows in cities using deep learning on satellite imagery
resources.description: Imagery2Flow uses deep learning to predict fine-scale movement between urban areas from satellite imagery. The researchers evaluate the model across ten large U.S. metropolitan areas and examine how its performance transfers across cities and time. The study connects learned visual representations with urban centrality, compactness, and sprawl, offering a potential way to support transport research where travel surveys are costly or incomplete. Its planning relevance includes mobility-data estimation and spatial comparison, while results show why geographical differences must be considered when transferring a model.

resources.description: Participants virtually explore street imagery and mark features such as curb ramps, surface problems, and blocked paths. The university-led platform pairs community contributions with machine learning and provides data in formats including GeoJSON and CSV. Project documentation identifies AI-supported validation of human labels and separate work on automatic feature labeling. For planners, it offers an operational example of accessible-mobility data collection, civic participation, open geospatial information, and human–AI collaboration in urban infrastructure assessment.

resources.title: Treepedia: street-level urban canopy mapping
resources.description: Treepedia estimates the share of greenery visible from street-level panoramas and presents mapped Green View Index values for selected cities. The project deliberately focuses on street views, so parks and other spaces outside available street imagery are not represented comprehensively. Its university page links relevant publications and historical Python code. The resource helps planning audiences interpret urban vegetation indicators, compare neighborhood streetscapes, and recognize the coverage and temporal limitations of imagery-derived environmental measures.

resources.title: LandCART: landscape cover analysis for land management
resources.description: UCLA co-developed LandCART with the Bureau of Land Management and NASA to make large, long-running vegetation datasets usable for land managers. The web tool maps categories including sagebrush, shrubs, grasses, dead vegetation, and bare ground, and uses machine learning to examine cover changes over time. It supports environmental planning questions such as habitat conservation and post-fire recovery. The linked UCLA article describes the February 2022 launch; it is not evidence of a newly released 2026 version.

resources.title: Hotspot Stoplight: biodiversity-aware urban growth assessment
resources.description: Penn designers developed Hotspot Stoplight with UN-Habitat to examine conflicts between urban expansion, biodiversity, and climate risk. Scripts link public geospatial datasets to machine-learning models that classify land and predict cover change at a 30-meter resolution. Risk and suitability layers help identify places requiring closer investigation before growth decisions. The team visited sites around San José to ground-truth the outputs. This entry describes a tested planning-support prototype, rather than an official land-use designation or an automated development approval system.

resources.title: SMAGNet: AI flood mapping under cloud cover
resources.description: ASU’s SMAGNet system uses AI to combine radar and optical satellite observations for flood mapping. The approach addresses a common operational problem: clouds can obscure the imagery needed during severe storms. The university article describes a system designed for incomplete and imperfect real-world observations and potential use in directing emergency resources. This is an emerging university tool with prospective response applications; the source does not establish an operational emergency service or claim that it has already prevented losses during disasters.

resources.description: USC researchers built urban-tree mapping models using free National Agriculture Imagery Program photographs, reducing reliance on costly lidar or commercial imagery. The university reports code and a ready-to-use ArcGIS deep-learning model, tested in Boyle Heights and City Terrace and applied without retraining in San Francisco and Phoenix neighborhoods. The work informs the USC Urban Trees Initiative’s collaboration with Los Angeles partners. For planning practice, it provides an accessible workflow for identifying tree-cover gaps and informing targeted urban-forestry and heat-resilience investments.

The public notebook identifies Texas A&M contributor Debayan Mandal; CyberGISX is developed and maintained at Illinois. This entry treats the platform as a practical analytical workflow, with results requiring interpretation in local policy and hazard contexts.

resources.description: Tile2Net detects pedestrian infrastructure in orthorectified aerial imagery and converts those predictions into geographic polygons and connected centerline networks. The software helps address the absence of consistent sidewalk information in many cities. Official university reporting documents its use to map networks in New York, Washington, and Boston and its uptake by public-health researchers. Planning teams can inspect the open-source workflow and outputs while checking imagery quality, local model performance, and network topology before relying on generated data for investment decisions.

resources.title: Flow: reinforcement learning for mixed-autonomy traffic
resources.description: Flow provides traffic-control benchmarks, custom scenario tools, and interfaces between reinforcement-learning algorithms and traffic simulation. Berkeley’s project page demonstrates learned controllers for ring-road shockwaves, intersection spacing, and highway on-ramp disturbances. This makes it a practical workflow for exploring how a small share of automated vehicles could affect broader network performance. Its showcased results are simulation experiments, so planners and transport engineers should treat them as evidence for scenario analysis and controller research rather than assume equivalent real-world performance.

resources.description: CodeGREEN is offered by the University of Florida’s McTrans Center for developing and analyzing traffic-signal timing plans. The official product page describes AI modeling and optimization alongside a map interface, CSV data import, timing charts, heatmaps, and corridor time-space diagrams. Engineers can develop plans for different periods or events and review the outputs before implementation. resources.description: The Illinois CyberGIS Center provides a notebook resource that applies deep learning to hydrological streamline detection. It derives feature maps from lidar observations and uses a U-net segmentation model to distinguish channels, comparing the result with traditional machine-learning approaches. The workflow addresses limitations of delineating streams from topography alone and is relevant to watershed analysis, water-resource inventories, and flood mapping. This is an analytical implementation that requires suitable input data and validation, rather than a ready-made local flood warning service.

resources.description: OpenMapFlow packages the stages needed to turn Earth-observation data into dense geographic prediction maps: preparing labeled datasets, training deep-learning models, and deploying inference through cloud infrastructure. It can support settlement and land-cover analysis when users supply suitable labels and validate predictions locally.
